guide.title: Diving & Altitude Emergencies
guide.lead: Gas laws cause both. Divers who become ill after surfacing need 100% oxygen, lying flat, and a hyperbaric chamber. At altitude, the cure for anything serious is going down; drugs and bags only buy time.

sections.title: After a dive
rows: Arterial gas embolism
Within minutes of surfacing (usually under 10): collapse, stroke-like signs, seizures, chest pain
100% oxygen, lie flat, ABCs, rapid transport to a hyperbaric centre
Decompression sickness
Usually within 6 hours (up to 24): joint pain, itchy or marbled rash, numbness, weakness, breathlessness
100% oxygen, lie flat, fluids (oral if alert, IV per protocol), hyperbaric centre
Pneumothorax
Chest pain, breathlessness, reduced breath sounds
Oxygen; decompress a tension pneumothorax
Ear and sinus squeeze
Pain, blood, vertigo during descent
Usually minor; hospital if vertigo or deafness
notes: Lying flat replaced head-down or left-side positioning. Bring the dive profile and computer. Air transport: fly low or in a pressurised cabin.

sections.title: Altitude illness
rows: Acute mountain sickness
Headache plus nausea, fatigue or dizziness, 6–12 hours after ascent; normal neuro exam
Stop ascending, rest, simple pain relief; descend if worse. Acetazolamide per protocol
High-altitude cerebral oedema
Ataxia (can't walk heel-to-toe), confusion, drowsiness
Descend now; oxygen; dexamethasone 8 mg, then 4 mg every 6 hours
High-altitude pulmonary oedema
Breathless at rest, cough, crackles, low SpO₂, worse at night
Descend now; oxygen; keep warm, minimise exertion; nifedipine ER 30 mg every 12 hours
notes: Descend 300–1000 m or until symptoms resolve. Portable hyperbaric bag if descent is impossible.

quiz.q: Diver surfaces from a deep dive and within 2 minutes collapses with right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Most likely?
options: Arterial gas embolism: 100% oxygen, lie flat, hyperbaric centre
Heart attack: aspirin and nearest ED
quiz.explanation: Symptoms within minutes point to gas embolism.

quiz.q: 8 hours after arriving at a ski resort: headache 4/10, nausea, fatigue, normal walking. Most likely?
options: Acute mountain sickness: stop ascending, rest, pain relief
quiz.explanation: No ataxia, no breathlessness at rest.

quiz.q: Diver with deep shoulder and elbow pain and an itchy marbled rash 20 minutes after a repeat dive; normal neuro exam. Diagnosis and care?
options: Decompression sickness (mild): 100% oxygen, lie flat, fluids, hyperbaric assessment
quiz.explanation: Joint and skin symptoms; check neuro function repeatedly.

quiz.q: Climber at 4300 m: severe headache, vomiting, can't walk a straight line, drowsy; lungs clear. Plan?
options: High-altitude cerebral oedema: descend now, oxygen, dexamethasone 8 mg
Acute mountain sickness: acetazolamide and rest

flashcards.question: Gas embolism vs decompression sickness timing
flashcards.answer: Gas embolism: within minutes of surfacing (usually under 10), often sudden collapse. DCS: usually within 6 hours, up to 24.

flashcards.question: Most important prehospital treatment in diving illness
flashcards.answer: 100% oxygen, as high a concentration as possible, for the whole transport.

flashcards.question: Pulmonary barotrauma
flashcards.answer: Breath-holding on ascent ruptures alveoli: gas embolism, pneumothorax, or mediastinal and subcutaneous emphysema.

flashcards.question: Definitive treatment for DCS and gas embolism
flashcards.answer: Recompression in a hyperbaric chamber. Before it: 100% oxygen, lie flat, fluids, treat pneumothorax, bring the dive computer.

flashcards.question: Three altitude illnesses
flashcards.answer: AMS: headache plus nausea, fatigue or dizziness; normal neuro. HACE: AMS plus ataxia or confusion. HAPE: breathless at rest, cough, crackles, low SpO₂.

flashcards.question: Treatment of HACE and HAPE
flashcards.answer: Descend 300–1000 m. HACE: oxygen, dexamethasone 8 mg then 4 mg every 6 hours. HAPE: oxygen, nifedipine ER 30 mg every 12 hours. Portable hyperbaric bag if stuck.

flashcards.question: Nifedipine in HAPE
flashcards.answer: Lowers pulmonary artery pressure, the driver of HAPE. Second line to descent and oxygen.

flashcards.question: Lake Louise Score
flashcards.answer: Rates headache, GI symptoms, fatigue and dizziness (0–3 each). AMS: headache with a total of 3 or more after recent ascent.

critical.scenario: Diver surfaces from a 50-minute dive to 18 m with a safety stop. 3 minutes later he loses consciousness on deck and has a brief seizure. A hyperbaric centre is farther than the local hospital.
critical.question: Diagnosis and transport?

options.t: Arterial gas embolism: 100% oxygen, lie flat, ABCs, transport toward the hyperbaric-capable centre (or stabilise locally if unstable and transfer)

critical.explanation: Contact a diving medicine service for advice.
critical.kpi: Recognizes arterial gas embolism and chooses a hyperbaric destination

critical.scenario: Hut at 3800 m on day 3: breathless at rest, productive pink cough, crackles, SpO₂ 68%. Descent requires a 4-hour hike at night.
critical.question: Plan?

options.t: HAPE: oxygen, keep warm and still, nifedipine ER; portable hyperbaric bag if available; descend as soon as safely possible

options.f: Exertion worsens HAPE: carry if possible.

critical.explanation: Descent is definitive; the rest buys time.
critical.kpi: Manages high-altitude pulmonary oedema when descent is delayed

critical.scenario: Diver flies home 6 hours after a day of repeat dives. On landing: numb legs, difficulty urinating, back pain.
critical.question: What is this, and the plan?

options.t: Spinal decompression sickness (worsened by flying): 100% oxygen, lie flat, fluids, urgent hyperbaric centre

options.f: Neuro deficits after diving and flying mean DCS.

critical.explanation: Flying soon after diving lowers pressure and enlarges bubbles.
